lessons.title: What it really costs

blocks.text: Read the trade-off

Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative given up. Workshop A's week can produce 60 chairs or 20 tables, so each table uses the time that would have made 60 ÷ 20 = 3 chairs. On a straight frontier that rate never changes, and the frontier's slope is the trade-off itself. Workshop B, whose week makes only 40 chairs, gives up 2 chairs per table.
Inside, on or beyond

Making 30 chairs uses half of Workshop A's week, which leaves time for 10 tables. Producing only 5 means idle time or waste: the point lies inside the frontier, and more of one good is available without giving up any of the other. Points on the frontier are productively efficient. A point such as 45 chairs with 12 tables lies beyond it and cannot be reached with today's workers, tools and methods.
Why the frontier bows

Resources differ in what they are good at. The first food comes from farmland and farm workers who were never much use in a factory, so few machines are lost. Later food pulls engineers and factory sites onto farms. Each extra 20 units of food costs 10, then 20, then 30, then 40 machines. That rising cost bends the frontier outward. A straight frontier would mean every resource is equally suited to both goods.
Price the next step

Divide what is lost by what is gained: 40 machines for 20 food is 2 machines per unit of food. The first step cost 10 machines for 20 food, only 0.5 each. An average over the whole frontier, 100 machines for 80 food, hides this. Decisions are about the next step, so the cost of the next step is the one to measure.

lessons.orientation: Measure opportunity cost along a production possibilities frontier, and see why it usually rises.

lessons.title: Who should make what

blocks.text: Faster is not the point

Ana is faster at both goods: she has an absolute advantage in each. That does not settle who should bake what. A cake costs Ana 12 ÷ 6 = 2 loaves of forgone bread; it costs Ben 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 loaves. Cakes are cheaper, in what is given up, when Ben makes them, even though Ana makes more cakes in a day.
Compare the costs

Comparative advantage means the lower opportunity cost. Ben's cake costs 1.5 loaves and Ana's costs 2, so Ben has the comparative advantage in cakes. The mirror image follows: a loaf costs Ana half a cake and Ben two-thirds of one, so Ana has the comparative advantage in bread. Two producers with different cost ratios each hold one comparative advantage.
Specialise, then swap

Specialising, Ben bakes 4 cakes, keeps 2 and trades 2 for 2 × 1.75 = 3.5 loaves. He ends with 2 cakes and 3.5 loaves, half a loaf more than splitting his own day gave him. Ana gains too: each cake costs her 1.75 loaves instead of the 2 she would forgo baking it. Any price between 1.5 and 2 loaves per cake helps both; at 2.5 Ana would rather bake her own.
Equal ratios, no gain

Cara and Dan both give up 2 loaves per cake. Cara is twice as productive at everything, yet no price leaves both better off: a rate below 2 loaves per cake hurts whoever sells cakes and a rate above 2 hurts whoever buys them. Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost. Differences in productivity alone create none.

lessons.orientation: Find comparative advantage from opportunity costs and show that specialisation and trade benefit both sides.

lessons.title: The next unit

blocks.text: One more hour

Marginal means one more. The café's first late hour adds £90 and costs £30; the second adds £70 for £35; the third adds £55 for £45. The fourth would add £40 but cost £50, so it would lower the café's net gain. Marginal benefit falls as late customers thin out, and marginal cost rises as staff move onto overtime. The best choice sits where the two meet.
Add up the gains

The three hours add £60, £35 and £10, a total of £105. A fourth would subtract £10 and a fifth another £30. Total net benefit peaks exactly where marginal net benefit turns negative, so comparing marginal values finds the best total without computing every total.
Costs that count

With costs of £50, £55 and £65, the third hour now loses £10, so two hours is best. A one-off cost already paid behaves differently. A £200 licence bought last month is sunk: it is the same whether the café opens no extra hours or five, so it changes no marginal comparison and should change no decision.
Averages mislead

Opening the fourth hour changes net benefit by £40 − £50 = −£10. The average benefit of the first four hours, (90 + 70 + 55 + 40) ÷ 4 = £63.75, sits well above £50, which tempts a wrong yes: the average includes hours that are being opened anyway. Only the extra hour's own benefit and cost decide the extra hour.

lessons.title: Demand meets supply

blocks.text: Read the demand curve

A demand curve records how much buyers plan to buy at each price, other things held constant. With Qd = 100 − 2P, a price of £15 gives 100 − 30 = 70 cups. Each £1 rise cuts planned purchases by 2 cups: price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, which is the law of demand. At £50 nobody buys.
Where plans agree

Equilibrium is the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied: 100 − 2P = 4P − 20, so 120 = 6P and P = £20. Supply slopes upward because a higher price covers the higher cost of extra output; here nothing is offered below £5. At £20 every cup offered finds a buyer, and nobody willing to pay £20 goes without.
The quantity traded

Substituting £20 gives 100 − 40 = 60 cups demanded and 80 − 20 = 60 supplied; checking both equations catches slips. The quantities are flows, cups per day, so the equilibrium is a rate of trade that lasts as long as the conditions behind both curves stay put.
Away from equilibrium

At £25 sellers offer 80 cups but buyers want only 50, a surplus of 30. Unsold stock pushes sellers to cut prices towards £20. At £15 the reverse happens: 70 cups wanted, 40 offered, a shortage of 30 that lets sellers raise prices. Excess supply and excess demand are the forces that pull a market back to equilibrium.

lessons.title: When the curves move

blocks.text: Along or across

A demand curve already answers 'how much at each price?', so a change in the good's own price is a movement along it: quantity demanded falls. The curve itself shifts only when something else changes, such as income, tastes, expectations, the number of buyers or the price of a related good. 'Demand' names the whole curve; 'quantity demanded' is one point on it.
Incomes rise

With demand shifted right, 130 − 2P = 4P − 20 gives P = £25 and Q = 80: price and quantity both rise. Coffee is behaving as a normal good, one whose demand rises with income. For an inferior good, such as the cheapest own-brand instant coffee, a rise in income shifts demand left instead.
A frost hits supply

100 − 2P = 4P − 44 gives P = £24, and Q = 100 − 48 = 52 cups. A fall in supply raises the price and lowers the quantity. Dearer inputs and bad harvests shift supply left; better technology and cheaper inputs shift it right, lowering the price and raising the quantity.
Two shifts at once

130 − 2P = 4P + 10 gives P = £20 again, while quantity rises from 60 to 90. When both curves shift right, quantity must rise but the price can go either way, depending on which shift is larger: with supply up by 60 instead, the price falls to £15. Work through each shift separately, then combine them.

lessons.orientation: Separate movements along a curve from shifts of it, and solve for the new equilibrium after a shift.

lessons.title: How strongly buyers respond

blocks.text: Measure the response

Elasticity is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. The midpoint method uses averages as the base, so the answer is the same whichever way the price moves. Quantity changes by 30 on an average of 50, or 60%; price changes by £2 on an average of £10, or 20%. Elasticity is 60% ÷ 20% = 3: demand is elastic, responding more than in proportion.
Revenue follows elasticity

Revenue rises from 11 × 35 = £385 to 9 × 65 = £585, a gain of £200. With elastic demand the percentage gain in tickets outweighs the percentage cut in price, so a price cut raises revenue. The rectangles show it: the new one loses a thin strip £2 high and gains a wide strip of 30 extra tickets.
Inelastic demand

Quantity changes by 10 on an average of 100, or 10%; price changes by £2 on an average of £5, or 40%. Elasticity is 10% ÷ 40% = 0.25, well below 1, so demand is inelastic: commuters with no alternative keep buying. Revenue falls from £570 to £420, because the price cut is proportionally far larger than the extra sales.
Unit elastic

Visits rise from 90 to 110 and revenue is £990 at both prices. Quantity changes by 20% on its average and price by 20% on its average, so elasticity is exactly 1. Along a straight demand line, elasticity changes: demand is elastic at high prices and inelastic at low ones, and revenue is largest at the unit-elastic midpoint.

lessons.title: Who gains from a sale

blocks.text: Value above the price

Each point on the demand curve is the most some buyer would pay for that cup. A buyer who values a cup at £35 and pays £20 keeps £15 of value she did not hand over: her consumer surplus. Producer surplus is the seller's version, the price received minus the lowest price the seller would have accepted.
The buyers' triangle

Add up every buyer's surplus and you get the triangle between the demand curve and the price line. Its base is the 60 cups sold; its height runs from the £20 price up to the £50 at which demand vanishes. Area = ½ × 60 × 30 = £900. A lower price would widen the base and raise the height at once.
The sellers' triangle

The supply curve shows the lowest price at which each cup would be offered, which is its marginal cost. The triangle between the price line and the supply curve has base 60 and height £20 − £5 = £15, so producer surplus is ½ × 60 × 15 = £450. Total surplus, £1,350, is the whole gain from trade in this market.
Lost trades

Each cup from the 40th to the 60th was worth more to a buyer than it cost a seller, and none of them is traded under the cap. The lost value is the triangle with base 20 and height £15: £150 of deadweight loss. Free exchange at equilibrium makes total surplus as large as possible, because every cup worth more than its cost changes hands and no cup worth less does.

lessons.orientation: Measure consumer and producer surplus as areas on the diagram and see why equilibrium makes their total largest.

lessons.title: What a tax takes

blocks.text: The wedge

A tax drives a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers keep. Sellers supply according to what they keep, P − 6, so supply becomes 4(P − 6) − 20. Setting that equal to 100 − 2P gives 6P = 144: buyers pay £24 and sellers keep £18. The price rises by £4, not the full £6. Who bears a tax depends on the curves, whoever hands the money over.
Revenue

Revenue is £6 × 52 = £312, the rectangle between the two prices across the cups still sold. It comes out of both surpluses: buyers pay £4 more on each of those 52 cups and sellers keep £2 less. The government's gain on those cups exactly matches what buyers and sellers lose on them.
The loss nobody collects

The 8 cups no longer sold were each worth more to a buyer than they cost to make; the tax stopped those trades. The lost surplus is a triangle with height £6 and base 8: ½ × 6 × 8 = £24. With straight-line curves, doubling a tax doubles both the height and the base, so the deadweight loss quadruples. Compare the £12 case.
Who really pays

Without the tax P = £25; with it buyers pay £27 and sellers keep £21. Here buyers bear £2 of the £6, against £4 in the coffee market. Demand is now more price-sensitive than supply, and the side that can more easily walk away bears less. Buyers' share is the supply slope over the sum of the slopes: 2 ÷ (4 + 2) of the tax.

lessons.orientation: Work out what a per-unit tax does to prices and revenue. Then measure the surplus it destroys and find who bears it.

lessons.title: Controls and spillovers

blocks.text: A ceiling that binds

A ceiling is a legal maximum price. Set at £12, below the £20 equilibrium, it binds: buyers want 76 cups and sellers offer 28, so 48 cups' worth of demand goes unmet. Only 28 cups change hands, fewer than the 60 at equilibrium, so the ceiling also destroys surplus. The shortage is rationed by queues, waiting lists or connections instead of price.
A floor that binds

At a £30 floor sellers offer 100 cups and buyers take 40, leaving 60 unsold. Minimum prices for farm goods have produced exactly this, with governments buying and storing the excess. A floor below the equilibrium price, or a ceiling above it, changes nothing at all.
Costs borne by others

Firms supply where the price covers their own marginal cost and ignore the £9 of damage each tonne does to people nearby. The market produces 60 tonnes. Counting the damage lifts the cost curve by £9: social supply 4(P − 9) − 20 meets demand at £26 and 48 tonnes. Each of the 12 extra tonnes costs society more than buyers value it.
A corrective tax

On the 12 overproduced tonnes, the gap between social cost and buyers' value grows from nothing at 48 tonnes to £9 at 60: a triangle of ½ × 12 × 9 = £54. A tax of £9 a tonne, equal to the marginal external cost, makes firms face the full cost and removes the loss. Arthur Pigou argued for such taxes in The Economics of Welfare (1920), and they carry his name.

lessons.title: Costs and the best output

blocks.text: Fixed and variable

Fixed cost, here £100 of rent, is paid whatever the output. Variable cost, q², grows with output and grows faster as the workshop gets crowded. At 5 units total cost is 100 + 25 = £125, so average total cost is £25. Spreading the fixed cost over more units pulls the average down at first; rising variable cost pushes it back up later.
Marginal meets average

Marginal cost is the cost of one more unit. While it is below the average, each new unit pulls the average down, as a low mark lowers a class average; once it is above, it pulls the average up. So MC crosses ATC at ATC's lowest point. Setting 2q = 100/q + q gives q² = 100 and q = 10, where both equal £20.
Produce to MR = MC

A firm maximises profit by producing up to the point where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. A competitive firm is a price-taker, so every unit adds the price, £30, to revenue. Below 15 units the next unit adds more revenue than cost; beyond 15 it adds less. This is the marginal rule from the start of the course, applied to output.
Profit as an area

Revenue is 30 × 15 = £450 and cost is 100 + 225 = £325, so profit is £125: the rectangle between the price and ATC (about £21.67) across 15 units. At £16 the best output is 8, with revenue £128 and cost £164, a loss of £36. The firm still produces in the short run, since shutting down would lose the whole £100 of rent.

lessons.title: One seller

blocks.text: Revenue from one more sale

A monopolist is the only seller, so to sell one more unit it must cut the price on every unit. At Q = 30 the price is £70, but the 31st unit adds only £39 to revenue: £69 for itself minus £1 lost on each of the other 30. For straight-line demand, the marginal revenue line starts at the same intercept and falls twice as fast.
Choose output, then price

MR = MC gives 100 − 2Q = 20 and Q = 40. Buyers will pay £60 for 40 units. The monopolist picks output where the MR line meets marginal cost, then charges the highest price the demand curve allows. Profit is (60 − 20) × 40 = £1,600, with no fixed cost.
Against competition

Competition drives price down to marginal cost: 100 − Q = 20 gives 80 units at £20. The monopoly sells half as much at three times the price. Buyers lose twice: they pay £40 more on the 40 units they still buy, and the other 40 units are never sold.
The monopoly triangle

Units 41 to 80 are each worth more to some buyer than the £20 they cost, yet none is produced. The lost value is a triangle with base 40 and height £40: ½ × 40 × 40 = £800. The £1,600 of profit is a transfer from buyers to the firm; the £800 is lost to everyone. Barriers to entry, such as patents and large economies of scale, let it persist.

lessons.title: Strategic choices

blocks.text: Fix the rival, compare

A payoff matrix lists every combination of choices and what each player earns. To find a best response, fix the rival's choice and compare your own payoffs. Against High, Low earns Alpha £14m instead of £10m by undercutting and taking customers. Against Low, Low earns £5m instead of £2m. Either way, Low pays Alpha more.
Dominant strategies

A dominant strategy is best whatever the other player does. Low beats High for Alpha against both of Beta's choices, and the payoffs are symmetric, so Low is dominant for Beta too. A player with a dominant strategy needs no forecast of the rival at all. The plug game has none: the best plug depends on the other maker's choice.
Nash equilibrium

Both firms choose Low and earn £5m each, £10m together, though both choosing High would earn £20m. Low/Low is a Nash equilibrium: neither firm gains by changing its own choice alone. This is a prisoner's dilemma, in which individually rational choices give an outcome both players rank below cooperation. It explains why cartels are fragile: each member gains by quietly undercutting.
Play it again

Alpha is undercut once, earning £2m, then matches Low for £5m in each of the next four rounds: £22m, while Beta earns £34m. Against another tit-for-tat player Alpha earns £10m every round, £50m in all. When a game repeats, the threat of retaliation can sustain cooperation that a one-off dilemma cannot, provided the future matters enough and the last round is not known in advance.

questions.prompt: Workshop A can make at most 60 chairs or 20 tables a week, trading one for the other at a constant rate. How many chairs does each extra table cost?
hints: Both maximums use the same week of work.
Ask how many chairs one table's share of the week could have made.
Divide the maximum number of chairs by the maximum number of tables.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 60 chairs ÷ 20 tables = 3 chairs per table.

questions.prompt: Workshop A can make at most 60 chairs or 20 tables a week at a constant rate. It makes 30 chairs and 5 tables. Where does that point lie?
hints: Work out how many tables the time left after 30 chairs could make.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Thirty chairs leave time for 10 tables, so 5 tables wastes capacity: the point is inside the frontier.

hints: Only the machines column matters for what is given up.
Find machines at both points.
Subtract the later figure from the earlier one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Machines fall from 70 to 40: 70 − 40 = 30 machines for 20 more food.

hints: Find the machines lost on this step.
Find the food gained on this step.
Divide the loss by the gain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 40 machines ÷ 20 food = 2 machines per unit of food.

questions.prompt: Priya has 12 hours of study time. An essay takes her 3 hours and a problem set takes 1.5 hours. What is the opportunity cost of one essay, measured in problem sets?

Ask how many problem sets fit into that same block.
Divide the essay's time by the time for one problem set.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 ÷ 1.5 = 2 problem sets per essay. The 12-hour total does not change the rate.

questions.prompt: In a day Ana can bake 12 loaves or 6 cakes. What is her opportunity cost of one cake, in loaves?
hints: A day of cakes and a day of bread use the same time.
Ask how much bread one cake's share of the day could have made.
Divide her loaves per day by her cakes per day.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 loaves ÷ 6 cakes = 2 loaves per cake.

questions.prompt: In a day Ana can bake 12 loaves or 6 cakes; Ben can bake 6 loaves or 4 cakes. Who has the comparative advantage in cakes? Give the name.

The comparative advantage belongs to whoever gives up less.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ben. A cake costs him 1.5 loaves against Ana's 2.

questions.prompt: Ben can bake 6 loaves or 4 cakes a day. Splitting his day he makes 2 cakes and 3 loaves. Instead he bakes only cakes and swaps 2 of them with Ana for 1.75 loaves each. How many more loaves does he end with than before?
hints: Find how many loaves the swap brings him.
He keeps the same number of cakes as before.
Subtract the loaves he used to bake from the loaves he receives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: He receives 2 × 1.75 = 3.5 loaves and keeps 2 cakes, so he has 3.5 − 3 = 0.5 loaves more.

questions.prompt: Cara can bake 8 loaves or 4 cakes a day; Dan can bake 4 loaves or 2 cakes. By how many loaves does their opportunity cost of a cake differ?
hints: Work out each person's loaves per cake.
Compare the two rates.
Subtract the smaller from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each gives up 8 ÷ 4 = 4 ÷ 2 loaves per cake, so the costs are equal and the difference is nothing.

Divide his reports per hour by his pages per hour.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Tom gives up 4 reports ÷ 1 page = 4 reports per page; Mira gives up only 2.

Count the hours worth more than the cost.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50, 40 and 30 each exceed 25; the fourth hour's 20 does not.

Set the equations equal and solve for P.
Substitute that price back into either equation.

questions.prompt: The price of coffee rises while nothing else changes. What happens on the demand diagram for coffee?
hints: Ask which variable is measured on the axis of the curve itself.

acceptedIdeas: A movement along the demand curve
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The good's own price is on the axis, so a change in it moves buyers along the curve; quantity demanded falls.

choices.label: A movement along the demand curve
A leftward shift of the demand curve
A rightward shift of the demand curve

questions.prompt: Incomes rise and coffee buyers want 30 more cups at every price, so demand becomes Qd = 130 − 2P. Supply stays Qs = 4P − 20. What is the new equilibrium price, in pounds?
hints: Set the new demand equal to the unchanged supply.
Collect the P terms on one side.
Divide the constant gap by the sum of the slopes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 130 − 2P = 4P − 20 gives 150 = 6P, so P = £25, up from £20.

questions.prompt: A frost destroys coffee crops and sellers offer 24 fewer cups at every price: Qs = 4P − 44. Demand stays Qd = 100 − 2P. What is the new equilibrium quantity, in cups?
hints: Set the original demand equal to the new supply.
Solve for the price first.
Substitute that price into the demand equation.

questions.prompt: Demand and supply each rise by 30 cups at every price: Qd = 130 − 2P and Qs = 4P + 10. By how many pounds does the equilibrium price change from its original £20?
hints: Find the new equilibrium price.
Set 130 − 2P equal to 4P + 10 and solve.
Subtract the old price from the new one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 130 − 2P = 4P + 10 gives P = £20, so the price is unchanged while quantity rises to 90.

questions.prompt: Tea and coffee are substitutes. If the price of tea rises, which way does the demand curve for coffee shift? One word.
hints: Some tea drinkers switch drinks.
Ask whether more or less coffee is wanted at each coffee price.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Right: some tea drinkers switch to coffee, so more coffee is wanted at every coffee price.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 120 − 3P and supply is Qs = 2P. A new factory adds 20 units of supply at every price. What is the new equilibrium price, in pounds?
hints: Write the new supply equation.
Set it equal to demand.
Solve for P.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Supply becomes Qs = 20 + 2P; 120 − 3P = 20 + 2P gives 100 = 5P, so P = £20, down from £24.

questions.prompt: When the price of a concert ticket falls from £11 to £9, the number sold rises from 35 to 65. Using the midpoint method, what is the absolute value of the price elasticity of demand?
hints: Divide the change in quantity by the average of the two quantities.
Divide the change in price by the average of the two prices.
Divide the first percentage by the second and drop the sign.

questions.prompt: Ticket sales rise from 35 at £11 to 65 at £9. By how many pounds does total revenue change?
hints: Revenue is price times quantity.
Compute revenue at each price.
Subtract the old revenue from the new.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Revenue goes from 11 × 35 = £385 to 9 × 65 = £585, a rise of £200.

questions.prompt: The price of a bus pass falls from £6 to £4 and passes sold rise from 95 to 105. What is the absolute midpoint elasticity of demand?
hints: Use the average quantity as the base for the quantity change.
Use the average price as the base for the price change.
Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage.

questions.prompt: Museum demand is Qd = 200 − 10P. The entry price falls from £11 to £9. By how many pounds does total revenue change?
hints: Find the quantity at each price.
Multiply each price by its quantity.
Subtract the old revenue from the new.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Visits rise from 90 to 110; revenue is 11 × 90 = £990 before and 9 × 110 = £990 after, so it does not change.

questions.prompt: Demand for a firm's product is inelastic. The firm raises its price. What happens to its total revenue?
hints: Compare the percentage change in price with the percentage change in quantity.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With inelastic demand, quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises, so price times quantity goes up.

choices.label: It rises
It falls
It stays the same

questions.prompt: The price of a phone case rises from £8 to £12 and quantity demanded falls from 110 to 90. Find the absolute midpoint elasticity of demand.
hints: Average the two quantities and the two prices.
Express each change as a share of its average.
Divide the quantity share by the price share.

questions.prompt: A buyer would pay up to £35 for a cup of coffee and buys it at the market price of £20. How much consumer surplus does she gain, in pounds?
hints: Consumer surplus is the gap between willingness to pay and the price paid.
Start from her maximum, not from the price.
Subtract the price from her maximum.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 4P − 20, so 60 cups sell at £20. Nobody buys at £50 or more. What is total consumer surplus, in pounds?
hints: Consumer surplus is a triangle above the price and below the demand curve.
Its height runs from the price up to the price at which demand reaches zero.
Take one half × base × height, with the quantity sold as the base.

questions.prompt: Supply is Qs = 4P − 20, so sellers offer nothing below £5. At the equilibrium price of £20 they sell 60 cups. What is total producer surplus, in pounds?
hints: Producer surplus is a triangle below the price and above the supply curve.
Its height runs from the lowest supply price up to the market price.
Take one half × quantity × that height.

questions.prompt: A rule caps coffee sales at 40 cups, below the free-market 60. For the 40th cup, buyers would pay £30 and sellers would accept £15. By how many pounds does total surplus fall?
hints: The lost units run from the 40th up to the 60th.
On each lost unit the loss is the gap between what buyers would pay and what sellers would accept.
Those gaps form a triangle, so take one half × base × height.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The lost cups form a triangle with base 60 − 40 = 20 and height 30 − 15 = 15: ½ × 20 × 15 = £150.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 80 − 2P and supply is Qs = 2P. What is consumer surplus at equilibrium, in pounds?
hints: Find the equilibrium price and quantity first.
Find the price at which quantity demanded falls to zero.
Take one half × quantity × (that price minus the equilibrium price).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 80 − 2P = 2P gives P = £20 and Q = 40. Demand reaches zero at £40, so CS = ½ × 40 × (40 − 20) = £400.

questions.prompt: Which area on a supply and demand diagram is consumer surplus?
hints: Consumer surplus belongs to buyers, so look for the curve that records buyers' values.

acceptedIdeas: Below the demand curve and above the price, up to the quantity sold
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Buyers gain the gap between what they would pay and the price they do pay. The demand curve records what they would pay.

choices.label: Below the demand curve and above the price, up to the quantity sold
Above the supply curve and below the price, up to the quantity sold
Below the supply curve, up to the quantity sold

questions.prompt: A £6 tax per cup is collected from coffee sellers. Demand is Qd = 100 − 2P, and supply in terms of the price sellers keep is Qs = 4P − 20. What price do buyers now pay, in pounds?
hints: Sellers keep the buyers' price minus the tax.
Replace P in the supply equation by (P − 6) and set it equal to demand.
Solve for the buyers' price.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Sellers keep P − 6, so 100 − 2P = 4(P − 6) − 20 gives 144 = 6P and P = £24.

questions.prompt: A £6 per-cup tax leaves 52 cups sold each day. How much tax revenue does it raise per day, in pounds?
hints: Revenue is the tax per unit times the units taxed.
Use the quantity after the tax, not before.
Multiply the two.

questions.prompt: A £6 per-cup tax cuts coffee sales from 60 to 52 cups a day. What is the deadweight loss, in pounds per day?
hints: The loss is a triangle between the curves over the units no longer sold.
Its height is the tax wedge and its base is the fall in quantity.
Take one half × base × height.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 120 − 4P and supply is Qs = 2P − 30. A £6 tax is collected from sellers. By how many pounds does the price buyers pay rise?
hints: Find the equilibrium price without the tax.
Find the buyers' price with the tax by replacing P with (P − 6) in supply.
Subtract the first price from the second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Without the tax 150 = 6P gives £25. With it, 120 − 4P = 2(P − 6) − 30 gives 162 = 6P, so £27: a rise of £2.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 90 − 3P and supply is Qs = 3P − 30. A £4 tax is collected from sellers. How many units are traded after the tax?
hints: Replace P in the supply equation by the price sellers keep.
Solve for the buyers' price.
Substitute that price into demand.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 90 − 3P = 3(P − 4) − 30 gives 132 = 6P, so buyers pay £22 and Q = 90 − 66 = 24.

questions.prompt: Without a tax 30 units are traded; a £4 per-unit tax cuts trade to 24 units. Both curves are straight lines. What is the deadweight loss, in pounds?
hints: Identify the units that are no longer traded.
The triangle's height is the tax per unit.
Take one half × base × height.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 4P − 20. A price ceiling of £12 is imposed. How large is the shortage, in cups?
hints: A ceiling below equilibrium is the price that actually applies.
Find quantity demanded and quantity supplied at the ceiling.
Subtract supply from demand.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At £12, Qd = 100 − 24 = 76 and Qs = 48 − 20 = 28, so the shortage is 76 − 28 = 48 cups.

questions.prompt: In the same market, Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 20, a price floor of £30 is set instead. How many cups are offered but not bought?
hints: A floor above equilibrium holds the price at the floor.
Find both quantities at the floor.
Subtract demand from supply.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At £30, Qs = 120 − 20 = 100 and Qd = 100 − 60 = 40: 60 cups go unsold.

questions.prompt: A paint market has demand Qd = 100 − 2P and supply Qs = 4P − 20, where supply reflects firms' own costs. Each tonne also causes £9 of pollution damage to people nearby. What quantity, in tonnes, maximises total surplus once that damage is counted?
hints: Add the external cost to the firms' own cost of each tonne.
In the supply equation, that means replacing P by (P − 9).
Set that social supply equal to demand and solve for quantity.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Social supply is 4(P − 9) − 20. Setting it equal to 100 − 2P gives 156 = 6P, so P = £26 and Q = 100 − 52 = 48 tonnes.

questions.prompt: In that paint market 60 tonnes are produced instead of the efficient 48, and each tonne does £9 of damage. What is the deadweight loss of the unregulated market, in pounds?
hints: The loss comes only from the overproduced tonnes.
On those tonnes the gap between social cost and value grows from zero to the external cost.
Take one half × base × height.

questions.prompt: A price ceiling of £30 is set in a market whose equilibrium price is £20. What happens?
hints: Ask whether the legal maximum stops the market price being reached.

acceptedIdeas: The ceiling does not bind, and nothing changes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The market price of £20 is already below the £30 maximum, so the ceiling has no effect.

choices.label: The ceiling does not bind, and nothing changes
A shortage appears
A surplus appears

questions.prompt: A per-unit tax set equal to the marginal external cost of an activity is named after which economist? Surname only.
hints: He succeeded Alfred Marshall as professor of political economy at Cambridge.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pigou: Arthur Cecil Pigou, in The Economics of Welfare (1920).

questions.prompt: A firm's total cost is TC = 100 + q², where £100 is fixed. What is average total cost at q = 5, in pounds?
hints: Average total cost is total cost divided by output.
Find total cost at that output first.
Divide by the number of units.

questions.prompt: With TC = 100 + q², marginal cost is MC = 2q and average total cost is 100/q + q. At what output is average total cost lowest?
hints: Average cost falls while the next unit costs less than the average.
The lowest point is where marginal cost equals average total cost.
Set the two expressions equal and solve for q.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ATC is lowest where MC = ATC: 2q = 100/q + q gives q² = 100, so q = 10.

questions.prompt: A competitive firm with MC = 2q sells at a market price of £30. What output maximises its profit?
hints: A price-taker's marginal revenue equals the price.
Produce while the next unit's revenue covers its marginal cost.
Solve price = 2q.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Marginal revenue is the £30 price; 30 = 2q gives q = 15.

questions.prompt: That firm has TC = 100 + q² and sells 15 units at £30 each. What is its profit, in pounds?
hints: Profit is total revenue minus total cost.
Revenue is price times quantity.
Total cost includes the fixed £100.

questions.prompt: Total cost is £50 at 0 units, £70 at 1, £85 at 2, £105 at 3 and £135 at 4. What is the marginal cost of the third unit, in pounds?
hints: Marginal cost is the change in total cost from one more unit.
Compare total cost at 2 units and at 3 units.
Subtract the smaller total from the larger.

questions.prompt: A competitive firm sells at £50 and its marginal cost is MC = 10 + 2q. What output maximises profit?
hints: Set price equal to marginal cost.
Move the constant to one side.
Divide by the slope of the marginal cost line.

questions.prompt: A monopolist faces demand P = 100 − Q, so marginal revenue is MR = 100 − 2Q. What is marginal revenue at Q = 30, in pounds?
hints: Substitute the quantity into the MR equation.
Double the quantity first.
Subtract that from the intercept.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: MR = 100 − 2 × 30 = £40, well below the £70 price.

questions.prompt: With demand P = 100 − Q and a constant marginal cost of £20, what price maximises the monopolist's profit, in pounds?
hints: Find the output where MR equals MC first.
Solve 100 − 2Q = MC.
Read the price from the demand curve at that output.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 − 2Q = 20 gives Q = 40, and the demand curve gives P = 100 − 40 = £60.

questions.prompt: If the market with demand P = 100 − Q and marginal cost £20 were competitive, price would equal marginal cost. What quantity would be sold?
hints: Set the demand price equal to marginal cost.
Solve 100 − Q = MC.
Compare the result with the monopoly output.

questions.prompt: In that market a monopoly sells 40 units at £60, while competition would sell 80 units at £20. What is the monopoly's deadweight loss, in pounds?
hints: The lost units lie between the two quantities.
On them, the gap between buyers' value and marginal cost shrinks from the markup to zero.
Take one half × base × height.

questions.prompt: A monopolist faces P = 60 − 2Q and has a constant marginal cost of £12. What is its profit-maximising quantity?
hints: With P = a − bQ, marginal revenue is a − 2bQ.
Write the MR equation for this demand curve.
Set MR equal to marginal cost and solve.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: MR = 60 − 4Q. Setting 60 − 4Q = 12 gives Q = 12, sold at P = 60 − 24 = £36.

questions.prompt: Compared with a competitive market with the same costs, a profit-maximising monopoly…
hints: Marginal revenue lies below the demand curve.

acceptedIdeas: sells less at a higher price
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It stops where MR = MC, short of where price meets marginal cost, and charges what demand allows for that smaller output.

choices.label: sells less at a higher price
sells more at a lower price
sells the same quantity at a higher price

questions.prompt: Alpha and Beta each set a High or Low price. If Beta sets High, Alpha earns £10m by also setting High and £14m by setting Low. If Beta sets Low, Alpha earns £2m with High and £5m with Low. When Beta sets High, how many £m more does Alpha earn by choosing Low?
hints: Fix Beta's choice and look only at that column.
Compare Alpha's two payoffs in it.
Subtract the smaller from the larger.

questions.prompt: In that game Alpha earns £10m or £14m against High (setting High or Low) and £2m or £5m against Low. Which price is a dominant strategy for Alpha? Answer High or Low.
hints: Find Alpha's best response to each of Beta's choices.
A dominant strategy is the best response to every choice the rival makes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Low: it pays Alpha more whatever Beta does.

questions.prompt: In that game both firms play their dominant strategy (Low) and each earns £5m; both choosing High would give them £20m together. What combined profit, in £m, do the firms earn at the Nash equilibrium?
hints: Find the cell where both play their dominant strategy.
Read both payoffs in that cell.
Add them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Low/Low gives £5m + £5m = £10m, half the £20m of High/High.

questions.prompt: The firms play that game for five rounds. Alpha plays tit for tat (High in round one, then copies Beta's last move); Beta always sets Low. With payoffs of £2m for a lone High, £14m for a lone Low and £5m each for Low/Low, what is Alpha's total profit, in £m?
hints: Write down both moves for each round.
In round one only Alpha sets High.
Add Alpha's payoff across all five rounds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Round one: Alpha High, Beta Low, so Alpha earns £2m. Rounds two to five: Low/Low, £5m each. Total 2 + 4 × 5 = £22m.

questions.prompt: Two phone makers choose a charging standard, A or B. If both pick A each earns 6; if both pick B each earns 4; if they pick differently each earns nothing. How many pure-strategy Nash equilibria does the game have?
hints: Check each of the four cells in turn.
In each cell, ask whether either maker gains by switching alone.
Count the cells where neither does.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A/A and B/B are both equilibria: in each, switching alone drops a maker to nothing. The mismatched cells are not.

questions.prompt: A game in which each player's dominant strategy leaves both worse off than cooperation is called the prisoner's what? One word.
hints: Picture two suspects questioned separately, each tempted to confess.

flashcards.front: A country can make at most 300 cars or 900 bicycles, at a constant rate of exchange between them. What is the opportunity cost of one car, in bicycles?
flashcards.back: 900 ÷ 300 = 3 bicycles per car.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 900 ÷ 300 = 3 bicycles per car.

flashcards.front: A frontier passes through (0 food, 50 tools), (10, 45), (20, 35), (30, 20) and (40, 0). Between 30 and 40 units of food, what is the opportunity cost per unit of food, in tools?
flashcards.back: Tools fall from 20 to 0 while food rises by 10: 20 ÷ 10 = 2 tools per unit of food.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Tools fall from 20 to 0 while food rises by 10: 20 ÷ 10 = 2 tools per unit of food.

flashcards.front: In a day a country's workers can make 50 shirts or 10 phones. What is the opportunity cost of one phone, in shirts?
flashcards.back: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 shirts per phone.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 shirts per phone.

flashcards.front: In an hour Uma picks 30 apples or 10 pears; Raj picks 20 apples or 10 pears. What is Raj's opportunity cost of one pear, in apples?
flashcards.back: 20 ÷ 10 = 2 apples per pear, below Uma's 3, so Raj has the comparative advantage in pears.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 20 ÷ 10 = 2 apples per pear, below Uma's 3, so Raj has the comparative advantage in pears.

flashcards.front: Successive adverts bring marginal benefits of £80, £60, £45 and £30. Each advert costs £40. How many adverts maximise net benefit?
flashcards.back: £80, £60 and £45 each cover £40; the fourth advert brings only £30.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: £80, £60 and £45 each cover £40; the fourth advert brings only £30.

flashcards.front: Three units bring marginal benefits of £12, £9 and £7, with marginal costs of £4, £5 and £8. What total net benefit does the best choice give, in pounds?
flashcards.back: Take the first two units: (12 − 4) + (9 − 5) = £12. The third would lose £1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Take the first two units: (12 − 4) + (9 − 5) = £12. The third would lose £1.

flashcards.front: Demand is Qd = 60 − 3P and supply is Qs = 2P − 10. What is the equilibrium price in pounds?
Demand is Qd = 90 − P and supply is Qs = 2P. At a price of £25, how large is the shortage?
flashcards.back: 65 units are demanded and 50 supplied: a shortage of 15.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 65 units are demanded and 50 supplied: a shortage of 15.

flashcards.front: Demand is Qd = 40 − P and supply is Qs = P. If demand rises by 10 units at every price, what is the new equilibrium quantity?
flashcards.back: 50 − P = P gives P = £25 and Q = 25.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50 − P = P gives P = £25 and Q = 25.

flashcards.front: Demand is Qd = 200 − 4P and supply is Qs = 6P. Supply falls by 30 units at every price. What is the new equilibrium price, in pounds?
The price of a snack falls from £5 to £3 and quantity demanded rises from 20 to 60. What is the absolute midpoint elasticity of demand?
flashcards.back: Quantity: 40 ÷ 40 = 100%. Price: 2 ÷ 4 = 50%. Elasticity = 100% ÷ 50% = 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Quantity: 40 ÷ 40 = 100%. Price: 2 ÷ 4 = 50%. Elasticity = 100% ÷ 50% = 2.

flashcards.front: Demand has an absolute price elasticity of 2. The price rises by 5%. By roughly what percentage does quantity demanded fall?
flashcards.back: %ΔQ ≈ elasticity × %ΔP = 2 × 5% = 10%.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: %ΔQ ≈ elasticity × %ΔP = 2 × 5% = 10%.

flashcards.front: A seller would accept no less than £12 for a chair and sells it for £20. What producer surplus does that sale create, in pounds?
Demand is Qd = 50 − P and supply is Qs = P − 10. What is producer surplus at equilibrium, in pounds?
flashcards.back: 50 − P = P − 10 gives P = £30 and Q = 20. Sellers offer nothing below £10, so PS = ½ × 20 × (30 − 10) = £200.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50 − P = P − 10 gives P = £30 and Q = 20. Sellers offer nothing below £10, so PS = ½ × 20 × (30 − 10) = £200.

flashcards.front: A £2 per-unit tax cuts the quantity traded from 50 to 44, with straight-line curves. What is the deadweight loss, in pounds?
Demand for a medicine is perfectly inelastic. What percentage of a per-unit tax on it do buyers bear?
flashcards.back: Buyers take the same quantity at any price, so the whole tax passes to them: 100%.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Buyers take the same quantity at any price, so the whole tax passes to them: 100%.

flashcards.front: Demand is Qd = 50 − P and supply is Qs = P − 10. A rent ceiling of £25 applies. How large is the shortage, in units?
flashcards.back: At £25, 25 units are demanded and 15 supplied: a shortage of 10.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At £25, 25 units are demanded and 15 supplied: a shortage of 10.

flashcards.front: Each tonne of output causes £5 of damage borne by people outside the market. What per-tonne tax makes producers face the full cost, in pounds?
flashcards.back: A Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal external cost: £5 a tonne.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A Pigouvian tax equal to the marginal external cost: £5 a tonne.

flashcards.front: A firm has fixed cost £60 and variable cost £8 for every unit. What is average total cost at 20 units, in pounds?
Making one more unit adds £25 to a firm's revenue and £31 to its cost. By how many pounds does profit change?
flashcards.back: £25 − £31 = −£6, so that unit should not be made.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: £25 − £31 = −£6, so that unit should not be made.

flashcards.front: A monopolist faces P = 80 − Q and a constant marginal cost of £20. What price does it charge, in pounds?
Demand is P = 50 − Q and marginal cost is a constant £10. What is the deadweight loss of monopoly, in pounds?
flashcards.back: Monopoly: 50 − 2Q = 10 gives Q = 20 at £30. Competition: Q = 40. DWL = ½ × 20 × 20 = £200.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Monopoly: 50 − 2Q = 10 gives Q = 20 at £30. Competition: Q = 40. DWL = ½ × 20 × 20 = £200.

flashcards.front: Payoffs (row, column) are Up/Left (3, 3), Up/Right (0, 5), Down/Left (5, 0) and Down/Right (1, 1). What does the row player earn in the Nash equilibrium?
flashcards.back: Down and Right are dominant, so the equilibrium is Down/Right and the row player earns 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Down and Right are dominant, so the equilibrium is Down/Right and the row player earns 1.

flashcards.front: Mutual cooperation pays 8 a round. A player who defects in round one against a grim-trigger rival earns 12 that round and 3 in every later round. What is the defector's total over 4 rounds?
flashcards.back: 12 + 3 × 3 = 21, against 4 × 8 = 32 from cooperating throughout.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 + 3 × 3 = 21, against 4 × 8 = 32 from cooperating throughout.
